H1.text: A sponge. A jellyfish. A cockroach.

H2.text: One has no organs at all. One has no head. One has six jointed legs. Yet all three are animals.

H3.text: Diya found all three on one page of her zoology book. She wants to be a doctor, so she asked: how do biologists sort animals this different?

H4.text: It is a big job. Over a million species of animals have been described so far.

H5.text: By the end, you will know the six body features biologists use to sort every animal.

B1.text: So how do you sort a million animals?

B2.text: Not by looks. A bat and a crow both fly, but the bat is a mammal and the crow is a bird.

B3.text: Biologists look at the body plan instead: how the body is built, from its cells to its layers and cavities.

B4.text: Features shared by many animals become the bases of classification. A basis is simply a feature we sort by.

Z1.text: Let's look closely at the three animals on Diya's page.

Z2.text: The sponge is a hollow body full of tiny pores, called ostia. Water flows in through them.

Z3.text: Inside is a central cavity, the spongocoel. The water leaves through one big opening on top, the osculum.

Z4.text: The jellyfish has a soft bell, with tentacles hanging from its edge. Cut it through the centre in any direction, and the halves match.

Z5.text: The cockroach has a head, a thorax and an abdomen, with jointed legs and long antennae.

Z6.text: Three very different bodies. To compare them fairly, biologists ask every animal the same six questions.

L1.text: Here are the six questions, one at a time.

L2.text: One. Level of organisation. Do the cells work loosely, or are they grouped into tissues, organs and organ systems?

L3.text: Two. Symmetry. Can a cut give two matching halves? And in how many directions?

L4.text: Three. Germ layers. How many layers does the embryo build, two or three? The embryo is the animal at its very earliest stage.

L5.text: Four. Coelom. Is there a body cavity between the gut and the body wall, lined by mesoderm, the middle germ layer?

L6.text: Five. Segmentation. Is the body built from repeated segments, like the rings of an earthworm?

L7.text: Six. Notochord. Does the embryo form a stiff rod along its back? This one splits animals into chordates and non-chordates.

L8.text: Biologists also compare body systems. For example, is the gut a bag with one opening, or a tube with two?

T1.text: Remember this. Animals are sorted by their body plan, not by their looks.

C1.text: Now let's run all three animals through the six questions.

C2.text: Question one. The sponge's cells work loosely, with no true tissues. That is the cellular level. The jellyfish has tissues. The cockroach has organ systems.

C3.text: Question two. The sponge has no symmetry. The jellyfish is radial: many cuts through the centre work. The cockroach is bilateral: only one cut gives matching left and right halves.

C4.text: Question three. The jellyfish builds two germ layers, so it is diploblastic. The cockroach builds three, so it is triploblastic.

C5.text: Question four. The cockroach has a coelom. The sponge and the jellyfish have no body cavity at all.

C6.text: Question five. The cockroach's body is segmented. The sponge and the jellyfish are not.

C7.text: Question six. None of the three forms a notochord. All three are non-chordates.

U1.text: But careful. One feature alone can fool you.

U2.text: A jellyfish is radial. It has two germ layers and no body cavity.

U3.text: A starfish is radial too. But it has three germ layers and a true coelom. And its larva, the young form, is bilateral.

U4.text: Your turn. A jellyfish and a starfish are both radial. Are they in the same phylum? Pause and decide.

U5.text: No! The starfish is an echinoderm, and the jellyfish is a coelenterate. The symmetry matched, but the germ layers and the coelom did not.

P1.text: Put the answers together, and they make one branching map of the animal kingdom.

P2.text: Cells only, with no tissues: the sponges, phylum Porifera.

P3.text: Two germ layers: the coelenterates and the comb jellies.

P4.text: Three germ layers, and then the cavity decides. No cavity in flatworms. A false cavity in roundworms. A true coelom in the rest.

P5.text: Last, the notochord splits the animals with a true coelom into non-chordates and chordates.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Diya finds an earthworm after the rain. Let's ask the six questions.

W2.text: Level: its organs work together as organ systems. Organ-system level.

W3.text: Symmetry: only one cut, down the middle, gives matching left and right halves. Bilateral.

W5.text: Coelom: yes, a true coelom. Segments: yes, its body is a chain of rings.

W6.text: Notochord: none. So the earthworm is a non-chordate, in phylum Annelida.

X2.text: Many students think a sponge is a plant, because it stays fixed in one place.

X3.text: But a sponge has no cell walls and no chlorophyll, and it takes in food from the water flowing through it. It is an animal, at the cellular level of organisation.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As statement or match questions that pair a group with its level, symmetry, germ layers or coelom.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Match each feature with the right animal group. Pause and solve.

A2.text: Sponges are at the cellular level. Coelenterates are diploblastic.

A3.text: Flatworms have no body cavity, so they are acoelomates. And the earthworm shows metameric segmentation.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Name the six features used to classify animals.

Y3.text: Two. Why is symmetry alone not enough to place an animal?

Y4.text: Three. Is a sponge a plant or an animal, and why?

N1.text: Next time: a crowd, a team and a machine. Can cells work alone, or must they team up? We find out in levels of organisation.
